title: LLMOps and Monitoring
summary: LLMOps applies DevOps discipline to LLM applications: monitoring quality and cost, tracing requests to debug failures, versioning prompts and models, and caching to save money. These operational skills separate hobby projects from production systems
content:
# LLMOps and Monitoring ##### ₹2.1 lakh, and nobody knew which feature spent it A B2B SaaS company in Hyderabad shipped three GenAI features in one quarter: a support assistant, a document summariser, and an email drafting tool. All three worked. Users liked them. The OpenAI invoice for March was ₹2,14,000 — up from ₹31,000 in January. The finance team asked the obvious question: which feature? Nobody could answer. There was one API key, shared across all three services. No per-feature tagging, no token logging, no traces. The dashboard showed one aggregate number. They spent two weeks instrumenting, and the answer was almost comic. The summariser was 84% of the spend, and 71% of *its* calls were duplicates — users re-summarising the same document repeatedly because the UI had no "recently summarised" list. A response cache and one UI change cut the monthly bill to ₹47,000. **They had built three products and zero observability.** That is the gap LLMOps fills: the operational discipline that makes an LLM application debuggable, affordable, and improvable rather than a black box that occasionally sends you a large invoice. ##### Why LLM systems need their own ops Traditional application monitoring watches latency, errors, and throughput. LLM systems need those *plus* four things that do not exist elsewhere: - **Non-determinism.** The same input can produce different outputs, so you cannot debug by reproducing. - **Quality has no status code.** A 200 response can contain a hallucination. Nothing in your HTTP metrics catches it. - **Cost is per request and highly variable.** A long document costs 40× a short question. - **Multi-step opacity.** A RAG answer passes through retrieval, reranking, prompt assembly, and generation. A bad answer could originate at any of them. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["LLMOps"] --> B["Observability
traces, logs, metrics"] A --> C["Versioning
prompts, models, indexes"] A --> D["Cost control
caching, routing, budgets"] A --> E["Feedback loops
ratings, eval sets"] B --> F["Debug what happened"] C --> G["Know what changed"] D --> H["Afford to run it"] E --> I["Improve over time"] ``` ##### Tracing A trace records the full execution of one request as a tree of nested spans. For a RAG query: retrieval, reranking, prompt assembly, generation — each with its own timing, input, and output. **This is the single highest-value thing you can add.** It answers "why was this answer wrong?" in seconds instead of hours, by showing you exactly which stage failed — the retrieval-versus-generation distinction from Day 35. ```python import os from langsmith import traceable from langsmith.wrappers import wrap_openai from openai import OpenAI os.environ["LANGCHAIN_TRACING_V2"] = "true" os.environ["LANGCHAIN_PROJECT"] = "hyderabad-support-assistant" client = wrap_openai(OpenAI()) # auto-traces every call @traceable(run_type="retriever", name="hybrid_retrieve") def retrieve(question: str, k: int = 25): return hybrid.search(question, k=k) @traceable(run_type="tool", name="rerank") def rerank_chunks(question: str, candidates: list, top_k: int = 5): return reranker_fn(question, candidates, top_k) @traceable(run_type="chain", name="rag_answer") def rag_answer(question: str, user_id: str, feature: str = "support"): candidates = retrieve(question) chunks = rerank_chunks(question, candidates) response = client.chat.completions.create( model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=build_prompt(question, chunks), temperature=0.0, metadata={"user_id": user_id, "feature": feature}, # ← per-feature tagging ) return {"answer": response.choices[0].message.content, "chunks": chunks, "usage": response.usage} ``` That `metadata={"feature": ...}` is what the Hyderabad team was missing. **Tag every call with the feature, the user, and the prompt version**, and cost attribution becomes a filter instead of a two-week investigation. If you prefer self-hosted, **Langfuse** offers the same capabilities and runs in your own infrastructure — often the right choice when your traces contain customer data subject to DPDP Act obligations. Rolling your own is viable for a smaller system: ```python import json, time, uuid, logging from contextlib import contextmanager logger = logging.getLogger("trace") @contextmanager def span(name: str, trace_id: str, **attrs): t0 = time.perf_counter() span_id = str(uuid.uuid4())[:8] error = None try: yield {"span_id": span_id} except Exception as exc: error = repr(exc) raise finally: logger.info(json.dumps({ "trace_id": trace_id, "span_id": span_id, "name": name, "duration_ms": round((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000, 1), "error": error, **attrs, })) ``` Structured JSON logs into any log aggregator gets you 70% of the value. ##### Metrics worth tracking | Category | Metric | Why | |---|---|---| | **Latency** | p50, p95, p99 end-to-end | p95 is what users complain about | | | Time to first token | The perceived-speed metric for streaming | | | Per-stage breakdown | Where is the time going? | | **Cost** | ₹ per request, per feature, per user | Attribution — the Hyderabad gap | | | Input vs output tokens | Output costs 3–5× more | | | Cache hit rate | Direct savings | | **Quality** | Refusal rate | Spikes mean retrieval broke | | | Citation rate | Grounding is working | | | Guardrail block rate | And its false-positive rate | | | User thumbs up/down | The only real signal | | **Reliability** | Error rate by type | 429s mean you need backoff or higher limits | | | Retry rate | Rising retries precede outages | **Track p95, not the mean.** A mean of 1.2 seconds with a p95 of 9 seconds means one user in twenty is having a bad time, and the mean hides it completely. ```python from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram REQUESTS = Counter("llm_requests_total", "Requests", ["feature", "model", "status"]) LATENCY = Histogram("llm_latency_seconds", "Latency", ["feature", "stage"], buckets=[0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 15, 30]) TOKENS = Counter("llm_tokens_total", "Tokens", ["feature", "model", "direction"]) COST = Counter("llm_cost_inr_total", "Cost in INR", ["feature", "model"]) CACHE = Counter("llm_cache_total", "Cache lookups", ["feature", "result"]) ``` ##### Caching The Hyderabad fix, and usually the largest single cost lever available. **Exact-match caching** — same prompt, same parameters, return the stored response. ```python import hashlib, json import redis r = redis.Redis(host="localhost", decode_responses=True) def cache_key(messages, model, temperature, version="v3"): payload = json.dumps({"m": messages, "model": model, "t": temperature, "v": version}, sort_keys=True) return "llm:" + hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()[:32] def cached_completion(messages, model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0.0, ttl=86400, feature="default"): # Only cache deterministic calls if temperature > 0: return call_llm(messages, model, temperature) key = cache_key(messages, model, temperature) hit = r.get(key) if hit: CACHE.labels(feature=feature, result="hit").inc() return json.loads(hit) CACHE.labels(feature=feature, result="miss").inc() result = call_llm(messages, model, temperature) r.setex(key, ttl, json.dumps(result)) return result ``` **The `version` in the cache key is essential.** Change your prompt and forget to bump it, and you serve stale responses generated by the old prompt indefinitely — a genuinely confusing bug to diagnose. **Semantic caching** goes further: if a new question is very similar to a cached one, reuse the answer. ```python def semantic_cached(question, threshold=0.95, feature="default"): q_vec = embedder.encode([question], normalize_embeddings=True)[0] hits = cache_collection.query(query_embeddings=[q_vec.tolist()], n_results=1) if hits["distances"][0] and (1 - hits["distances"][0][0]) >= threshold: CACHE.labels(feature=feature, result="semantic_hit").inc() return hits["metadatas"][0][0]["answer"] answer = generate(question) cache_collection.upsert(ids=[hashlib.sha256(question.encode()).hexdigest()[:16]], embeddings=[q_vec.tolist()], metadatas=[{"answer": answer, "question": question}]) return answer ``` **Set the threshold high — 0.95 or above.** At 0.85, "What is the notice period for the MSA?" and "What is the notice period for the NDA?" may collide, and you serve a confidently wrong cached answer. Semantic caching trades correctness for cost, and the exchange rate depends entirely on that threshold. **Provider prompt caching** is the third kind: OpenAI and Anthropic both discount repeated prefixes substantially. Structure your prompts with the long stable part first — system prompt, few-shot examples, retrieved context — and the variable part last, and you get this nearly for free. ##### Cost optimisation Roughly in order of impact: 1. **Route by difficulty.** Most queries do not need your best model. ```python def route(question: str, context_len: int) -> str: if len(question) < 120 and context_len < 2000: return "gpt-4o-mini" if requires_reasoning(question): return "gpt-4o" return "gpt-4o-mini" ``` Model routing routinely cuts costs 60–80% with negligible quality loss, because the distribution of query difficulty is heavily skewed toward easy. 2. **Cache** — as above. 3. **Trim prompts.** Every call pays for the full system prompt. Audit it; most are 30% padding. 4. **Cap `max_tokens`.** Output tokens cost several times input tokens. 5. **Retrieve fewer chunks.** Day 36 argued five good chunks beat twenty; that is a quality *and* a cost argument. 6. **Batch APIs** for non-urgent work — around 50% cheaper. 7. **Self-host** at steady high volume. A rented GPU running Llama beats per-token pricing past a certain point; compute your break-even. Enforce a budget in code, not just in the dashboard: ```python class BudgetGuard: def __init__(self, daily_limit_inr=2000.0): self.limit = daily_limit_inr def check(self, feature: str) -> None: spent = float(r.get(f"spend:{feature}:{today()}") or 0) if spent >= self.limit: raise BudgetExceeded(f"{feature} hit ₹{self.limit} daily cap") def record(self, feature: str, cost: float) -> None: k = f"spend:{feature}:{today()}" r.incrbyfloat(k, cost) r.expire(k, 172800) ``` ##### Prompt and model versioning Prompts are code. Version them, review them, and test them. ```python from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict import json, hashlib @dataclass(frozen=True) class PromptVersion: name: str version: str system: str user_template: str model: str temperature: float notes: str = "" @property def hash(self) -> str: return hashlib.sha256( json.dumps(asdict(self), sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()[:12] RAG_PROMPT = PromptVersion( name="rag_answer", version="v4", model="gpt-4o-mini", temperature=0.0, system="You answer using ONLY the provided context...", user_template="Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}", notes="v4: added explicit refusal phrase; v3 hallucinated on unanswerable Qs", ) ``` **Log `prompt_version` and `prompt_hash` with every request.** When quality drops on Tuesday, you can filter traces by version and see exactly which change caused it. Without this, you are guessing. Beyond prompts, version everything that affects output: the model name and snapshot (`gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18`, not just `gpt-4o-mini`), the embedding model, the vector index build, and the retrieval parameters. **Changing your embedding model silently invalidates your entire index** — a failure mode that produces mysteriously poor retrieval with no error anywhere. Run your Day 40 evaluation suite in CI on every prompt change. Block the merge if scores regress. ##### Latency and throughput Where the time goes in a typical RAG request: | Stage | Typical | Optimisation | |---|---|---| | Embedding the query | 10–40ms | Cache; use a smaller model | | Vector search | 5–50ms | Tune `ef_search`; reduce dimensions | | Reranking (25 candidates) | 50–150ms | Rerank fewer; smaller reranker | | LLM generation | 800–4000ms | **Dominant. Stream, or use a faster model** | | Guardrails | 50–200ms | Run rule checks first, LLM checks async | Generation dominates, which is why **streaming is the highest-impact latency work you can do** — it does not reduce total time but cuts time-to-first-token from 3 seconds to 300ms, and perceived speed is what users judge. Other levers: run retrieval and moderation concurrently with `asyncio.gather`, use async throughout (LLM calls are I/O-bound, so async workers scale far better than threads), and set aggressive timeouts with fallbacks. ##### Feedback loops Observability tells you what happened. Feedback tells you whether it was any good. ```python @app.post("/feedback") async def feedback(req: FeedbackRequest): record = { "request_id": req.request_id, "rating": req.rating, # "up" | "down" "reason": req.reason, # optional free text "ts": time.time(), } await store_feedback(record) if req.rating == "down": trace = await fetch_trace(req.request_id) await add_to_review_queue({**record, "trace": trace}) return {"status": "recorded"} ``` **The loop that makes a system improve:** 1. Collect thumbs up/down in the UI, tied to the request ID. 2. Every negative rating goes to a review queue **with its full trace**. 3. Review weekly, and classify: retrieval failure, generation failure, or coverage gap. 4. Add the hard cases to your Day 40 evaluation set. 5. Fix, verify against the eval set, ship. Step 4 is what compounds. **Your evaluation set should grow from production failures**, so it converges on the queries that actually break your system rather than the ones you imagined at build time. Expect low feedback volume — 1–5% of users rate anything. Supplement with implicit signals: did the user rephrase immediately (a bad answer), copy the response (a good one), or abandon the session? ##### Common mistakes - **One API key across all features**, making cost attribution impossible. - **No tracing**, so debugging a bad answer means re-running and hoping. - **Tracking the mean latency** instead of p95. - **No cache**, paying repeatedly for identical requests. - **Forgetting the prompt version in the cache key**, serving stale responses. - **Semantic cache threshold too low**, returning confidently wrong cached answers. - **Unversioned prompts**, making regressions untraceable. - **Changing the embedding model without rebuilding the index.** - **No budget enforcement in code** — the dashboard alert arrives after the spend. - **Collecting feedback but never reviewing it.** - **Logging full prompts containing PII** without retention limits, a DPDP Act problem. - **Using the largest model for everything** instead of routing by difficulty. ##### Hands-on: instrument, then optimise Your practical task adds tracing and response caching. Set up LangSmith or Langfuse, tag calls by feature, and run twenty queries — then open the trace view and find your slowest span. It will almost certainly be generation, which tells you where optimisation effort belongs. Add the exact-match cache, re-run the same twenty queries twice, and measure the hit rate and the cost difference. Seeing ₹4.20 become ₹0.00 on the second run makes the case immediately. The mini project builds a monitoring dashboard for latency, cost, tokens, and feedback. Streamlit is fine for this and quick. The panel that matters most is **cost by feature over time** — that single chart is what the Hyderabad team lacked. Add a table of the ten most recent thumbs-down responses with links to their traces, because that turns your dashboard from a status display into a work queue. The assignment analyses a week of logs and proposes three optimisations. Generate realistic synthetic logs if you do not have real ones — a few thousand requests with a skewed cost distribution and some duplicates. Then quantify each proposal: "42% of calls are exact duplicates; a 24-hour cache saves ₹18,000/month," "p95 latency is 8.2s driven by reranking 50 candidates; reducing to 20 saves 90ms at a 1-point recall cost," "the summariser uses gpt-4o for 3,200 calls averaging 180 input tokens; routing those to gpt-4o-mini saves ₹31,000/month." Numbers with reasoning are what get a proposal approved. ##### Key takeaways - **Tag every LLM call with feature, user, and prompt version** — cost attribution and quality debugging both become filters instead of investigations. - **Tracing is the highest-value addition**: it tells you within seconds whether a bad answer came from retrieval, reranking, or generation. - **Caching and model routing are the two biggest cost levers**, routinely cutting spend 60–80%; include the prompt version in the cache key and keep semantic thresholds above 0.95. - **Prompts are code.** Version them, log the version with every request, and run your evaluation suite in CI so regressions block the merge. - **Feed production failures back into your evaluation set** — that loop is what makes the system genuinely improve rather than merely stay up.
practical_task_reference: Add tracing to your deployed app with LangSmith and implement response caching to reduce repeated API costs.
mini_project_reference: Instrument your GenAI app with a monitoring dashboard tracking latency, cost, token usage, and user feedback.
